# Precocious puberty

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric endocrinology and metabolism > Precocious puberty*

[Original Article Link](/library/Pv0WZR)

---

## Summary

Precocious <u>puberty</u> is the appearance of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years of age in boys. Precocious <u>puberty</u> is classified as <u>central precocious puberty</u>, resulting from early <u>gonadotropin-releasing hormone</u> (<u>GnRH</u>) secretion causing activation of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u>, or <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u>, resulting from sex <u>hormone</u> production that is not driven by <u>GnRH</u> secretion. <u>Central precocious puberty</u> may be <u>idiopathic</u> or caused by <u>CNS</u> pathology or genetic syndromes. Causes of <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> include increased sex <u>hormone</u> production from <u>adrenal</u> or gonadal tumors, <u>functional ovarian cysts</u>, <u>exogenous</u> <u>steroid</u> use, and <u>hypothyroidism</u>. Clinical evaluation involves a focused history and <u>physical examination</u>, including a <u>pediatric growth</u> assessment and <u>sexual maturity rating</u>, to distinguish precocious <u>puberty</u> from <u>benign pubertal variants</u>. Initial diagnostic evaluation includes laboratory testing (<u>gonadotropin</u> and <u>sex hormone levels</u>) and a <u>bone age</u> assessment. Targeted testing to determine the underlying cause is based on clinical presentation and initial results. Management is based on the underlying cause. <u>GnRH</u> analogs may be considered in some patients with <u>central precocious puberty</u>.

---

## Classification

### By location [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)




#### Central precocious puberty




* Caused by early onset of <u>GnRH</u> secretion

* Early activation of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u> → abnormally early initiation of pubertal changes → early development of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u>

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (10:1) [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)

* The sequence and rate of progression of <u>pubertal development</u> are symmetrical and align with those in <u>normal puberty</u>, but <u>puberty</u> occurs at an early age. [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[5]](/library/lXVvyG0)





#### Peripheral precocious puberty




* Early development of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> caused by an increase in sex <u>hormones</u> that is not driven by <u>GnRH</u> secretion

* The sequence and rate of progression of <u>pubertal development</u> may be incomplete, asymmetrical, or discordant from those in <u>normal puberty</u>. [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[5]](/library/lXVvyG0)





### By <u>phenotype</u> [[6]](/library/dxdovH0)




#### Isosexual precocious puberty




* Early development of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> that match the individual's biological sex

* Can occur in central and <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u>





#### Heterosexual precocious puberty




* Early development of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> that are discordant with the individual's biological sex

* Can occur in <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> (e.g., <u>McCune-Albright syndrome</u>, <u>Leydig cell tumors</u>, <u>congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>)

---

## Etiology

### Etiology of central precocious puberty [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[6]](/library/dxdovH0)[[7]](/library/IZVY1G0)




* <u>Idiopathic</u> (most common cause in girls)

* <u>CNS</u> lesions 

* <u>Intracranial tumors</u> (e.g., <u>hypothalamic hamartoma</u>, <u>optic pathway glioma</u>)

* <u>Hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Brain injury</u> (e.g., <u>traumatic brain injury</u>, <u>radiation injury</u>)

* Intracranial infections (e.g., <u>encephalitis</u>, <u>meningitis</u>)

* Genetic syndromes: <u>neurofibromatosis type 1</u>, <u>tuberous sclerosis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Boys are more likely than girls to have an identifiable cause of <u>central precocious puberty</u> (e.g., <u>CNS</u> lesions). [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[6]](/library/dxdovH0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Hypothalamic hamartoma</u> is the most common <u>CNS</u> lesion in <u>central precocious puberty</u>. [[6]](/library/dxdovH0)




### Etiology of peripheral precocious puberty [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[6]](/library/dxdovH0)




* Increased <u>androgen</u> production

* <u>Congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>

* Adrenocortical tumors

* <u>Androgen</u>-producing gonadal tumors (e.g., <u>Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor</u>, <u>Leydig cell tumor</u>)

* Increased <u>estrogen</u> production

* <u>McCune-Albright syndrome</u>

* <u>Functional ovarian cyst</u>

* Tumors that produce <u>β-hCG</u>  [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[6]](/library/dxdovH0)[[8]](/library/rXVfzG0)

* <u>Embryonal carcinoma</u>

* <u>Testicular choriocarcinoma</u>

* <u>Primary hypothyroidism</u>

* Exposure to <u>exogenous</u> <u>steroids</u> (e.g., <u>OCPs</u>, <u>estrogen</u>-containing creams, <u>testosterone</u> gel)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Central precocious puberty</u> has a central cause (e.g., <u>hypothalamic</u> lesions) and high <u>GnRH</u> levels, while <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> has a peripheral cause (e.g., <u>germ cell tumors</u>) without elevated <u>GnRH</u> levels.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Obesity</u> is associated with early <u>pubertal development</u>. See "Factors affecting timing and progression of <u>puberty</u>." [[9]](/library/L-dwBs0)[[10]](/library/GZVB1G0)

---

## Clinical evaluation

The clinical presentation depends on the underlying condition.




### Focused history [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)




* <u>Pubertal development</u>

* Age of onset of <u>secondary sexual characteristic</u> development, e.g.:

* Pubic and axillary <u>hair</u>

* Body odor

* <u>Breast</u> development

* Testicular development

* Sequence and pattern of development

* Symmetry in development of <u>breasts</u> and <u>testes</u>

* Complete vs. incomplete development (e.g., isolated <u>premature thelarche</u>, <u>adrenarche</u>, or <u>menarche</u>)

* Additional signs of <u>puberty</u> (e.g., voice change, <u>acne</u>, <u>vaginal bleeding</u>)

* Associated features of an underlying cause

* Neurological symptoms (e.g., <u>headache</u>, <u>vision</u> changes)

* <u>Symptoms of hypothyroidism</u> or <u>clinical features of thyrotoxicosis</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Personal <u>medical history</u>

* History of <u>brain tumor</u> or <u>head trauma</u>

* Cancer treatments (e.g., <u>chemotherapy</u>, radiation)

* Sex <u>steroid</u> use (e.g., <u>OCPs</u>, topical <u>estrogen</u> or <u>testosterone</u>)

* <u>Family history</u>: timing of parental <u>puberty</u>  [[4]](/library/lubvrv)

* Environmental exposures: endocrine-disrupting chemicals (e.g., lavender oil, phthalates)





### Focused examination [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)




* <u>Pediatric growth</u> assessment

* Standard <u>pediatric growth parameters</u> (e.g., height, weight, and <u>BMI</u>)

* <u>Growth velocity</u>

* <u>Midparental height</u>

* Evaluation for <u>physical changes during puberty</u>

* <u>Sexual maturity rating</u>  [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)

* Facial and axillary <u>hair</u>

* <u>Acne</u>

* Evaluation for underlying cause

* Abdominal and testicular examination: for gonadal tumors

* Vaginal examination to assess for signs of:

* <u>Estrogen</u> exposure (e.g., dull pink vaginal <u>mucosa</u>, <u>vaginal discharge</u>)

* <u>Virilization</u> (e.g., clitoromegaly)

* <u>Skin examination</u>: for <u>café au lait macules</u> (seen in <u>McCune-Albright syndrome</u>, <u>neurofibromatosis</u>)

* <u>Thyroid examination</u>

* <u>Neurological examination</u>: for suspected <u>CNS</u> pathology





> [!TIP]
> Children with precocious <u>puberty</u> may have accelerated growth (i.e., increased <u>growth velocity</u> or predicted height inconsistent with <u>midparental height</u>) in <u>adolescence</u> but typically have shorter than average stature in adulthood due to early closure of the <u>epiphyseal plates</u>. [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)




> [!TIP]
> Consider other <u>causes of tall stature</u> in children with accelerated growth but no signs of <u>pubertal development</u>. [[11]](/library/oCd0GH0)

---

## Diagnostics

### Approach [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[12]](/library/ECd8FH0)




Evaluate for precocious <u>puberty</u> if <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> manifest before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years of age in boys.




* Suspected benign pubertal variant : Consider observation for 3–6 months before diagnostic testing.

* Multiple and/or progressive development of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u>: Obtain initial studies, including early morning <u>gonadotropin</u> levels and <u>bone age</u> <u>radiography</u>. 

* <u>LH</u> > 0.3 IU/L: targeted testing for <u>etiology of central precocious puberty</u> [[4]](/library/lubvrv)

* <u>LH</u> < 0.3 IU/L with suspected <u>central precocious puberty</u>: <u>GnRH stimulation test</u>

* Prepubertal <u>LH</u> levels

* Suspected <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u>: targeted testing for <u>etiology of peripheral precocious puberty</u>

* Suspected benign pubertal variant: observation

* Diagnostic uncertainty: Refer to <u>endocrinology</u> for further evaluation.





> [!TIP]
> Patients with normal initial <u>laboratory studies</u> and isolated examination findings suggesting <u>benign pubertal variants</u> can be observed for 3–6 months before further workup. [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)




> [!TIP]
> The diagnostic approach to precocious <u>puberty</u> in children with <u>obesity</u> is the same as in children with <u>normal body weight</u>. [[10]](/library/GZVB1G0)




### Initial diagnostic studies [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* <u>LH</u> and <u>FSH</u>

* Typically increased in <u>central precocious puberty</u>

* Prepubertal levels suggest <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> or a benign pubertal variant.

* <u>Testosterone</u> (boys) or <u>estradiol</u> (girls) 

* Typically increased in both central and <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u>

* <u>Estradiol</u> > 100 pg/ml suggests an ovarian source (e.g., <u>ovarian tumor</u>). [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)





#### <u>Bone age</u> <u>radiography</u>  [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)




* Most commonly performed as <u>x-ray</u> of nondominant hand and wrist

* Advanced <u>bone age</u> (> 2.5 <u>standard deviations</u>) compared to chronological age suggests central or <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> rather than benign pubertal variant [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)





> [!TIP]
> Advanced <u>bone age</u> is common in children with <u>obesity</u>, which limits the utility of <u>bone age</u> <u>radiography</u> in distinguishing between precocious <u>puberty</u> and <u>benign pubertal variants</u>.[[10]](/library/GZVB1G0)




### Additional diagnostic studies [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[3]](/library/L8bwMv)




Obtain additional testing based on clinical presentation and initial diagnostics. Consult a specialist (e.g., <u>endocrinology</u>) as needed.




#### Suspected <u>central precocious puberty</u> despite <u>LH</u> < 0.3 IU/L [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)




* GnRH stimulation test

* <u>LH</u> elevation after <u>GnRH</u> stimulation: <u>central precocious puberty</u>

* No <u>LH</u> elevation after <u>GnRH</u> stimulation: <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> or benign pubertal variant

* <u>Pelvic</u> imaging: Consider in girls to assess uterine and ovarian volume in the case of diagnostic uncertainty.





#### Targeted testing for underlying cause




* <u>Central precocious puberty</u> and/or suspected <u>CNS</u> pathology: <u>MRI</u> <u>sella</u> (without and with IV contrast; or without IV contrast)  [[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[12]](/library/ECd8FH0)[[13]](/library/hoXcb_)

* <u>Signs of hypothyroidism</u> or <u>signs of hyperthyroidism</u>: <u>TSH</u>

* <u>Signs of hyperandrogenism</u>: serum <u>DHEA-S</u>, <u>17-hydroxyprogesterone</u>

* Suspected gonadal <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Ultrasound</u> <u>pelvis</u> or <u>testes</u>

* <u>β-hCG</u> in boys with suspected <u>germ cell tumors</u>

* Suspected <u>adrenal</u> <u>tumor</u>: <u>adrenal</u> imaging





> [!TIP]
> <u>CNS</u> imaging is recommended in all boys and in girls < 6 years of age with <u>central precocious puberty</u>. Use <u>shared decision-making</u> to determine the need for imaging in girls 6–8 years of age. [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[12]](/library/ECd8FH0)

---

## Management

Manage precocious <u>puberty</u> in consultation with a pediatric specialist as appropriate (e.g., <u>endocrinology</u>, <u>neurology</u>, <u>surgery</u>). [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)




### Management of <u>central precocious puberty</u> [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[16]](/library/r-dfAs0)




* <u>GnRH agonists</u> (e.g., <u>leuprolide</u>, buserelin, <u>goserelin</u>, <u>histrelin</u>) [[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[12]](/library/ECd8FH0)

* Indications

* Preservation of height potential  [[4]](/library/lubvrv)

* Promotion of psychosocial well-being

* Prevention of early <u>menarche</u> and sexual maturity  [[4]](/library/lubvrv)

* Duration of therapy: based on patient's height potential and ability to tolerate <u>puberty</u>

* <u>Expectant management</u> may be considered in the absence of indications for <u>GnRH agonists</u>.

* Management of <u>CNS</u> lesions, if present

* Management of associated psychological <u>stress</u> (e.g., <u>anxiety</u>) as necessary





> [!TIP]
> Childhood <u>obesity</u> is not a contraindication to <u>GnRH agonists</u> in children with precocious <u>puberty</u>. [[10]](/library/GZVB1G0)




### Management of <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u> [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)




Treat the underlying cause, e.g.:




* <u>Hormone</u>-producing <u>tumor</u>: <u>surgery</u> [[6]](/library/dxdovH0)

* <u>Congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>: <u>cortisol</u> replacement (see “Treatment of <u>congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>”)

* <u>Ovarian cysts</u>

* Spontaneous resolution is common.

* <u>Surgery</u> may be indicated for complications.

* See “<u>Management of ovarian cysts</u>” for details.

---

## Mimics

### Benign variants of puberty [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[17]](/library/7ub4sv)




* <u>Benign pubertal variants</u> involve isolated development of <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> and prepubertal pattern of linear growth.

* Observation over 3–6 months is usually appropriate. [[4]](/library/lubvrv) [[3]](/library/L8bwMv)[[17]](/library/7ub4sv)

* Children with progressive <u>pubertal development</u> and/or rapid linear growth during this period should be evaluated for precocious <u>puberty</u>. [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)

### Minipuberty of <u>infancy</u> [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[20]](/library/EgV8CF0)




* Transient increase in <u>estradiol</u> or <u>testosterone</u> caused by temporary activation of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u> after <u>birth</u>

* Manifests with the following ∼ 1 week after <u>birth</u> (peaks at 2–3 months of age):

* Girls: <u>breast</u> development, minimal <u>vaginal bleeding</u>

* Boys: <u>self-limited</u> penile growth

* <u>Acne</u>

* Typically resolves by age ∼ 6 months in boys and 2–4 years in girls.





### Pubic <u>hair</u> of <u>infancy</u> [[2]](/library/qgVCwF0)[[4]](/library/lubvrv)[[19]](/library/VxdGvH0)[[21]](/library/7gV49F0)




* Uncommon condition characterized by the development of pubic <u>hair</u> at ∼ 8 months of age in the absence of any other signs of <u>puberty</u> or <u>hyperandrogenism</u>

* Often manifests as thin, straight <u>hair</u> on the labia or <u>scrotum</u>

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* Rule out exposure to <u>exogenous</u> <u>hormones</u> or endocrine disruptors.

* Diagnostic studies are not routinely required if there are no signs of pubertal progression or abnormal <u>growth velocity</u>.

* Typically resolves spontaneously by 1–2 years of age
